newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore refiners upbeat on less export from west.
newsitem.headline: Singapore refiners upbeat on less export from west.

text.p: Beleaguered Singapore refiners are optimistic of finding more buyers for their surplus products as competition from cheaper western cargoes wanes because of higher prices there, refining sources said on Wednesday.
"We had problems selling our cargoes at competitive prices in the past, but now, as prices in the west are much higher, traders are not able to bring in cargoes from there," one refiner said.

Exports of western-origin oil products, such as gas oil (diesel), jet fuel and fuel oil, were prevalent earlier this year as Asian prices were much higher than in the west. These western cargoes, brought in by oil trading firms, have been a mainstay in Asia over the past three years, traders said.
Such exports had cut into the Singapore refiners' market share in Asia and some were forced to lower operating rates as it was not profitable to run crude units at optimal capacity.

Refiners in Asia were also finding it harder to sell their products after the startup of new refineries earlier this year in Thailand and South Korea, which added nearly one million barrels per day in capacity.
But now lower inventories in the west, coupled with strong demand, had caused prices there to rise above those in Asia, which stopped exports to this region, said a trader with an oil major.

Refining margins have since returned to the black, after being in the red for most of July and August, and refiners are confident they would continue to make money in the fourth quarter -- a peak demand period.
The refiners said they were not bothered that prices in Asia were below those in the west as the absolute values of these products are high and give good returns.
Singapore gas oil prices are now around $27.60 per barrel, close to the post-Gulf War high of around $28.30, despite being $6-8 per tonne below those quoted in London.
This meant surplus jet fuel from the U.S. Gulf Coast and the Caribbean is being first shipped to the West Coast rather than North Asia, a trader said.
The refiner said prices on the West Coast were sometimes high enough to attract exports from Singapore and South Korean refiners.
But players were aware that an unusually cold winter would easily open the arbitrage for jet-kerosene fuel exports from the United States to North Asia, he said.
In the first half of this year, Asian prices were $5-10 per tonne higher than in the west, opening the export arbitrage for traders.
"Asia is becoming self-sufficient for gas oil and there will be less opportunity for traders to move product from west-to-east. But a reverse arbitrage might open," one trader said.
The sources said they also saw changes in the jet fuel market, where prices on the U.S. West Coast are about $2.00 per barrel higher than in Singapore.
Fuel oil prices, however, have not dipped below that of the west but are only $4-5 per tonne more, not enough for traders to ship cargoes over.
"You need prices in Singapore to be about $10-13 above the west for the arbitrage to work," a trader said.
